source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility, pKa 9.99); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Alcohols and Phenols

name: Sodium ethoxide solution
description: The salt formed when sodium takes the hydrogen from an alcohol's OH group. It is strongly basic — far more so than sodium hydroxide — which is itself the proof that ethanol is a very weak acid: the weaker the acid, the stronger the base it leaves behind.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Alcohols, reaction with sodium

name: Sodium phenoxide solution
description: What phenol becomes once sodium hydroxide has taken its hydrogen. The negative charge left on the oxygen is spread out over the whole benzene ring rather than sitting on one atom, and that sharing is precisely why phenol can lose its hydrogen when ethanol cannot.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Phenols, acidity

name: Ethanal (acetaldehyde)
description: An ALDEHYDE: the carbonyl carbon still carries a hydrogen, and that hydrogen is what makes it easy to oxidise further. It boils at only 21 °C, which is why the practical instruction is to distil it off as it forms — leave it in the flask and the oxidising agent will take it straight on to the acid. It is also the compound the body makes from alcohol, and the one responsible for a hangover.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, boiling point); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aldehydes and Ketones

name: Propanone (acetone)
description: A KETONE: the carbonyl carbon sits between two carbon groups and has no hydrogen of its own. That single structural difference is why it resists oxidation — there is nothing on that carbon to take off without breaking the chain — and it is what every test distinguishing aldehydes from ketones actually detects. Familiar as nail varnish remover.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aldehydes and Ketones

name: Ethanoic acid (acetic acid)
description: The acid in vinegar, and a genuinely WEAK one — a 1 M solution sits at about pH 2.4 where 1 M hydrochloric acid is near 0, because only a small fraction of its molecules give up their hydrogen at any moment. Weak is not the same as dilute: this is a concentrated solution of a weak acid. It is still acidic enough to fizz with a carbonate, which phenol is not, and that difference places it firmly above phenol in acidity.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, pKa 4.76); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Carboxylic Acids

name: Sodium ethanoate solution
solubility: very soluble (about 46 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: The salt of a weak acid and a strong base, so its solution is ALKALINE rather than neutral — the ethanoate ion takes hydrogen ions back from the water. Mixed with ethanoic acid it makes the standard buffer solution, which resists a change in pH when acid or alkali is added.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Carboxylic Acids, salts and buffers

name: Ethyl ethanoate
solubility: slightly soluble (about 8 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: An ESTER, and the reason this reaction is memorable: it smells sweet and fruity, like pear drops, where both the acid and the alcohol it came from smell of nothing pleasant at all. Esters are what give fruit and flowers much of their scent, and they are used as flavourings and as solvents — including in nail varnish and glue.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Carboxylic Acids, esterification

name: Tollens' reagent
description: Ammoniacal silver nitrate — a colourless solution holding silver as the diammine complex, ready to be reduced back to the metal. It is made fresh immediately before use and never stored, because on standing it forms silver nitride, which is dangerously explosive when dry. Any leftover must be acidified and washed away at once.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aldehydes and Ketones, Tollens' test; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass of the complex)

name: Fehling's solution
description: A deep blue solution of copper(II) held in alkali by tartrate ions, which stop it precipitating as the hydroxide. It is a MIXTURE, not a single compound, so it has no molar mass of its own — the figure given is that of the copper(II) sulfate it is built from, and no more than that should be read into it. Like Tollens' it is mixed from its two stock bottles immediately before use.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aldehydes and Ketones, Fehling's test; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass of copper(II) sulfate)

name: Copper(I) oxide
description: Brick-red precipitate, and copper in the unusual +1 state rather than its familiar +2. Watching a deep blue solution throw down a red solid is what makes Fehling's test easy to read even for a student who has never seen it before. The same reaction was once used to test urine for sugar, because glucose has an aldehyde group and reduces the copper in exactly this way.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Aldehydes and Ketones, Fehling's test

name: Phosphorus pentachloride
description: The standard laboratory test for an —OH group: add it to the substance and steamy, choking fumes of hydrogen chloride come off at once. Alcohols, phenols and carboxylic acids all give the fumes; an ester, an aldehyde or a ketone gives none. It must be kept absolutely dry, because it attacks water just as readily as it attacks an —OH group and the reaction with water is violent.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Carboxylic Acids, reaction with PCl5

name: Phosphoryl chloride
description: The by-product left behind when phosphorus pentachloride is used to make an acid chloride. It is not the point of the reaction, but it has to go somewhere, and a student who writes the equation without it has not balanced anything. Also called phosphorus oxychloride.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Carboxylic Acids

name: Ethanoyl chloride
description: An ACID CHLORIDE, and the most reactive of the carboxylic acid derivatives. The chlorine pulls electrons hard away from the carbonyl carbon and leaves it wide open to attack, which is why this fumes in moist air, hisses with water, and turns an alcohol into an ester in seconds without heat or catalyst. It is the reagent you reach for when the direct route from the acid is too slow. Also called acetyl chloride.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, boiling point 52 °C); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Carboxylic Acids and their derivatives

name: Ethanoic anhydride
description: Two ethanoic acid units joined through a shared oxygen, and the second rung down the reactivity ladder. It does everything the acid chloride does — water, alcohols, ammonia — but more slowly and more manageably, and it gives no corrosive hydrogen chloride. That gentleness is why industry prefers it: it is the reagent used to make aspirin.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Carboxylic acid derivatives

name: Ethanamide
solubility: very soluble (about 200 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: An AMIDE, and the bottom rung of the reactivity ladder — so unreactive that it takes prolonged boiling with acid or alkali to break it apart. It contains nitrogen and looks as though it ought to be a base like ammonia, and it is NOT: the carbonyl group beside the nitrogen holds that lone pair away, so ethanamide is neutral. The same C—N link, repeated thousands of times, is the peptide bond that holds a protein together, and its stubbornness is why proteins survive at all. Also called acetamide.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Carboxylic acid derivatives, amides

name: Glyceryl tristearate (a fat)
description: An ordinary fat, and structurally nothing more exotic than an ESTER — three long fatty-acid chains joined to one molecule of glycerol. Every fat and oil in food is built this way; the only real difference between a solid fat and a liquid oil is how straight those chains are. Because it is an ester, it can be hydrolysed by alkali, and that single fact is the whole of soap making.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Macromolecules, lipids and saponification

name: Soap (sodium stearate solution)
description: The sodium salt of a long-chain acid, and the reason it works is that its two ends want opposite things: the charged —COO⁻ head dissolves happily in water while the long hydrocarbon tail refuses to and buries itself in grease instead. Its solution is alkaline, because it is the salt of a weak acid and a strong base — which is why soap feels slippery and why it is harsh on wool and silk.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Macromolecules, soaps and detergents; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass)

name: Glycerol
description: A thick, sweet, harmless liquid with three —OH groups, recovered as the valuable by-product of soap making. It holds on to water, which is why it turns up in hand creams, toothpaste and cough syrup, and it is also the starting material for nitroglycerine — the same molecule, put to very different use.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Macromolecules, lipids

name: Soap scum (calcium stearate)
description: The grey curdy solid that appears instead of a lather when soap meets hard water. Calcium has two positive charges where sodium had one, so it grips two soap molecules at once and the result will not dissolve. Every scrap of soap that ends up as scum is soap that did no washing — which is what hard water actually costs you, and it is the ring left round the bath.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Macromolecules, action of hard water on soap

name: Synthetic detergent solution
description: Built to the same two-ended plan as soap — water-loving head, grease-loving tail — but with a sulfonate head in place of the —COO⁻. That swap is the entire point: the calcium salt of a sulfonate stays dissolved, so a detergent lathers in hard water where soap only makes scum. It is also close to neutral rather than alkaline, so it is safe on wool and silk. The cost is environmental: the branched-chain versions resisted breakdown and foamed up rivers, which is why straight-chain detergents replaced them.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Macromolecules, soaps and detergents

name: Glucose solution
solubility: very soluble (about 91 g per 100 mL at 25 °C)
description: The sugar your body actually runs on, and a REDUCING SUGAR — it carries an aldehyde group, so it does everything ethanal did with Tollens' and Fehling's. Two other things worth knowing about it. It dissolves freely yet does not conduct at all, which makes it the standard example of a non-electrolyte: it dissolves as whole molecules, not as ions. And in solution almost all of it curls into the six-membered ring drawn here, with only a trace open-chain form at any moment — yet that trace is enough for the whole sample to react, because as fast as it is used up more ring opens to replace it.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Macromolecules, carbohydrates

name: Sucrose solution (table sugar)
solubility: very soluble (about 200 g per 100 mL at 25 °C)
description: Ordinary table sugar: one glucose joined to one fructose. It is a NON-reducing sugar, and the reason is worth seeing rather than memorising — the link between the two halves is made through exactly the carbon that would otherwise open into an aldehyde. With that carbon tied up, there is nothing left to reduce Fehling's, and the test comes out blank. Break the link and both tests turn positive at once.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Macromolecules, disaccharides

name: Invert sugar solution
description: What sucrose becomes when it is hydrolysed: an equal mixture of glucose and fructose, and the real name the food industry uses for it. It is a MIXTURE of two sugars rather than one compound — the molar mass given is honest only because glucose and fructose happen to be isomers with the same formula. Both halves are now free to open into their reducing forms, so this reduces Fehling's where the sucrose it came from did not. Honey is largely invert sugar, which is why it is sweeter than table sugar.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Macromolecules, hydrolysis of sucrose; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass of the hexoses)

name: Sodium gluconate solution
description: What is left of the glucose once Fehling's or Tollens' has oxidised it: the aldehyde group has become a —COO⁻ group, and everything else about the molecule is unchanged. It is a salt rather than a sugar, so unlike the glucose it came from it conducts electricity — dipping the conductivity tester before and after the test shows the change directly.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Macromolecules, oxidation of glucose

name: Starch solution
solubility: forms a colloid rather than a true solution
description: Hundreds of glucose units joined into long chains — how a plant stores the sugar it makes. It has no single molar mass, and that is not a gap in this app's data: different starch molecules genuinely have different lengths, so the question has no one answer. Nor does it truly dissolve; it forms a milky colloid, which is why it looks cloudy where a sugar solution is clear. Because every reducing group is locked into the chain, starch fails Fehling's test completely.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Macromolecules, polysaccharides

name: Starch–iodine complex
solubility: stays dispersed in the starch colloid
description: The intense blue-black that appears the instant iodine meets starch. Strictly it is not a compound at all: the starch chain coils into a helix and iodine molecules thread into the tube down its middle, and it is that trapping — not any bond — that produces the colour. Two things follow that a student can check. Warm it and the colour vanishes as the helix unwinds; cool it and the colour comes back. And no colour ever appears if the starch has already been broken into glucose, which is exactly how you tell that a hydrolysis has finished.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Macromolecules, iodine test for starch

name: Egg albumin solution
description: Egg white in water, and a straightforward protein to work with. A protein is a chain of amino acids joined by exactly the amide link met in the last batch — which is why the test for a protein is really a test for that link. It has no single molar mass because different protein molecules are different lengths. Its shape matters as much as its formula: the chain is folded into a particular arrangement held by weak forces, and everything a protein does depends on keeping that fold.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Macromolecules, proteins

name: Biuret reagent
description: A little copper(II) sulfate in plenty of sodium hydroxide — a MIXTURE, like Fehling's, and with no molar mass of its own. It is pale blue on its own and turns violet with anything containing peptide links. It is named after biuret, a small molecule that gives the same colour for the same reason, and not after any part of a protein.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Macromolecules, biuret test for proteins

name: Copper–peptide complex
description: The violet colour of a positive biuret test. Copper(II) is being gripped by the nitrogen atoms of several peptide links at once, and it is that grip which shifts the colour from pale blue to violet. The test detects the LINK rather than any particular amino acid, so a single amino acid on its own gives nothing — you need at least two links, which means at least three amino acids joined together. The deeper the violet, the more protein is present, and that is how protein is measured quantitatively.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Macromolecules, biuret test for proteins

name: Coagulated protein
description: A cooked egg white. The chain of amino acids is entirely intact — not one peptide link has been broken — but the folding that held it in shape has been shaken apart, and the unfolded chains have tangled into each other and come out of solution. That is DENATURATION, and the reason it cannot be undone by cooling is simply that the tangle will not sort itself out again. Because the links survive, a biuret test on a boiled egg white is still positive.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Macromolecules, denaturation of proteins

name: Urea
solubility: very soluble (about 108 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: The most used fertiliser on earth and the backbone of Pakistan's chemical industry, at 46 % nitrogen — more than any other solid fertiliser. Chemically it is a double amide: one carbonyl carbon carrying two —NH₂ groups, so everything learnt about ethanamide applies to it. It matters historically too. Making it from ammonia and carbon dioxide, both lifeless minerals, was the first time anyone built a compound previously known only from living things, and it ended the idea that organic chemistry needed a special vital force.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Common chemical industries, fertilisers

name: Ammonium sulfate solution
solubility: very soluble (about 75 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: A nitrogen fertiliser, and one with a catch worth knowing. It is the salt of a WEAK base and a STRONG acid, so its solution is acidic rather than neutral — the opposite way round from sodium ethanoate. Used year after year it steadily sours the soil, which is why fields treated with it eventually need liming. It also supplies sulfur, which crops need too, so it is not simply a worse choice than urea.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Common chemical industries, fertilisers

name: Silica (sand and clay)
description: Sand, quartz and most of ordinary clay. Its formula looks like carbon dioxide's and the two could hardly behave less alike: CO₂ is a gas of separate small molecules, while SiO₂ is one endless network in which every silicon is bonded to four oxygens and every oxygen bridges two silicons. That difference is why sand melts near 1700 °C and carbon dioxide does not melt at all. Breathing the fine dust over years causes silicosis, which is why it is wetted down on building sites.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, melting point); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Group IVA elements and the cement industry

name: Cement clinker
solubility: reacts slowly with water rather than dissolving
description: The dark grey nodules that come out of a cement kiln, ground to powder to make the cement sold in bags. Its most important property is one people underestimate: mixed with water it is strongly ALKALINE, about pH 12.5, which is why wet cement causes serious burns that are often not felt until hours later. Bricklayers lose skin to it every year.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Common chemical industries, cement; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density of tricalcium silicate)

name: Set cement
description: Hardened cement: a mat of interlocking crystals grown through the water that was mixed in. It has no single formula and no single molar mass, because the amount of water taken up varies — which is honest data, not missing data. The everyday belief that cement hardens by DRYING is simply wrong: it hardens by reacting with water, it sets perfectly well underwater, and concrete left to dry too fast ends up weaker rather than stronger.
source: Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Common chemical industries, setting of cement

name: Alum solution (aluminium sulfate)
solubility: very soluble (about 36 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: What is added at the first stage of nearly every waterworks in the world, and what a village household uses when it rubs a lump of phitkari round a pot of muddy water. Its solution is distinctly ACIDIC even though neither aluminium nor sulfate looks like an acid, because the small, highly charged Al³⁺ ion pulls hard enough on the water around it to force hydrogen ions off. That same pull is what makes it useful: it is halfway to becoming aluminium hydroxide already.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Environmental chemistry, water treatment

name: Aluminium hydroxide floc
description: A soft, open, jelly-like solid — a FLOC rather than an ordinary precipitate, and the difference is the whole point. A dense precipitate would drop straight to the bottom and leave the water as dirty as before; this one forms slowly as a loose sticky mesh through the whole depth of the water, gathering clay particles, bacteria and colour into itself as it sinks. What is filtered off afterwards is far more than the aluminium hydroxide alone.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Environmental chemistry, coagulation in water treatment

name: Tetrachlorocuprate(II) solution
description: The same copper ion as in blue copper sulfate, wearing different ligands. Four chlorides have pushed the six water molecules off, and with them go both the colour and the SHAPE — the aqua ion is octahedral with six ligands, this is tetrahedral with four. Chloride is a bigger ligand and only four will fit. Both facts matter: the colour of a transition metal ion is a property of the whole complex, not of the metal alone, which is why the same copper can look blue, green or deep violet depending only on what is bonded to it.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — tetrahalometallates; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass)

name: Hexaaquacobalt(II) solution
description: Cobalt(II) with six water molecules around it, octahedral, and pale pink. This is what cobalt chloride looks like in ordinary dilute solution, and it is one half of the most quoted equilibrium in inorganic chemistry. Add concentrated chloride and it turns blue; dilute it again and the pink returns. Nothing is created or destroyed in either direction — the same cobalt simply swaps one set of ligands for another.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — aqua ions and ligand substitution; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass)

name: Tetrachlorocobaltate(II) solution
description: The other half of the cobalt equilibrium: tetrahedral, four chlorides, and an intense blue. The colour change from pink is so complete and so easily reversed that this is the standard demonstration of Le Chatelier's principle. It is also, incidentally, why cobalt chloride paper tests for water — the blue dry paper turns pink the moment water displaces the chloride.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — tetrahalometallates and the cobalt(II) equilibrium; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass)

name: Nickel(II) chloride solution
description: Nickel(II) in water, green from the hexaaqua ion. Nickel is the most common cause of metal allergy in the world — it is why cheap earrings make some ears sore — and the sensitisation happens through skin contact with nickel salts exactly like this one. Handle with gloves, which is good practice with any transition metal salt but genuinely important here.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility); Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — nickel(II) chemistry

name: Dimethylglyoxime solution
solubility: soluble in ethanol, sparingly in water
description: A CHELATING ligand — one molecule with two nitrogen atoms placed exactly right to grip a single metal ion at two points at once, like a crab's claw. That two-point grip is far harder to break than two separate ligands would be, and it is the reason chelates are so stable. Dimethylglyoxime happens to fit nickel almost perfectly and very few other ions, which makes it one of the most selective reagents in analytical chemistry.
source: Vogel's Textbook of Quantitative Chemical Analysis 6th ed. — gravimetric determination of nickel; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass)

name: Nickel dimethylglyoximate
description: A striking rose-red solid, and one of the few precipitates clean enough to be weighed directly. Two dimethylglyoxime molecules grip one nickel between them, the whole thing is flat and square, and because it is uncharged it will not dissolve in water at all. Its composition is exact and reproducible, which is what makes gravimetric analysis possible: filter it, dry it, weigh it, and you know how much nickel was in the sample to four figures.
source: Vogel's Textbook of Quantitative Chemical Analysis 6th ed. — gravimetric determination of nickel; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass)

name: Tetrahydroxoaluminate solution
description: What aluminium hydroxide becomes in excess alkali: a soluble complex ion, and the proof that aluminium hydroxide is AMPHOTERIC. It dissolves in acid, as any base does, and it dissolves in alkali too, which no ordinary base does. This is also the basis of the Bayer process for purifying bauxite: the aluminium oxide dissolves in hot alkali and the iron oxide impurity does not, so the two separate cleanly on that single difference.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — amphoteric hydroxides and the Bayer process; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass)

name: Zinc hydroxide
description: A white gelatinous solid that looks almost exactly like aluminium hydroxide, and telling the two apart is a standard problem in qualitative analysis. Both are amphoteric, so both dissolve in excess sodium hydroxide and neither result distinguishes them. The test that does work is ammonia: zinc dissolves in it and aluminium does not, because zinc forms an ammine complex and aluminium has no such chemistry.
source: Vogel's Textbook of Qualitative Inorganic Analysis 5th ed. — separation of the aluminium and zinc groups; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density)

name: Tetrahydroxozincate solution
description: Zinc hydroxide dissolved in excess alkali, and proof that zinc hydroxide is amphoteric just as aluminium's is. On its own this result cannot tell zinc from aluminium, because both give a colourless solution that looks identical. Chemistry is often like this: a test that gives the same answer for two things has told you something, but not what you wanted to know.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — zincate chemistry; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass)

name: Tetraamminezinc(II) solution
description: Zinc held by four ammonia molecules, and the answer to the aluminium problem. Zinc forms this readily; aluminium forms nothing of the kind, so its hydroxide simply sits there in ammonia unchanged. Note that this complex is COLOURLESS where the copper equivalent is deep blue — zinc has a full d shell with no room for the electron jumps that give transition metal complexes their colour, which is the standard argument for not counting zinc as a true transition metal.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — zinc ammine complexes and the d10 configuration; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass)

name: Sodium dichromate solution
description: Orange, and the acid form of the chromate–dichromate pair. Two chromate units have joined through a shared oxygen, exactly the way two ethanoic acid units join in an anhydride. The chromium stays at +6 throughout, so this is NOT a redox change however dramatic the colour looks — a point worth being firm about, because the orange-to-yellow shift is easily mistaken for one. Chromium(VI) in any form is carcinogenic.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — chromate–dichromate equilibrium; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass)

name: Sodium thiosulfate solution (hypo)
solubility: very soluble (about 70 g per 100 mL at 20 °C)
description: Known in every darkroom as hypo. Its structure is a sulfate ion with one oxygen replaced by sulfur, and that swapped sulfur is what does the work: it is a soft donor atom, and soft donors bind soft metal ions like silver far more strongly than hard ones like calcium. That single principle explains why hypo dissolves silver bromide and why it is used to mop up spilt iodine, and it is also the reagent titrated against iodine in every iodometric determination.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — hard and soft acids and bases; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility)

name: Dithiosulfatoargentate(I) solution
description: Silver, which is famously insoluble as the halide, held in solution by two thiosulfate ions. This complex is what carried photography for a century and a half: the unexposed silver bromide on a film has to be washed away or the picture goes black in daylight, and nothing else removes it so cleanly. It is also why photographic waste is worth collecting — the silver is recovered from exactly this solution.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — silver thiosulfate complexes; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass)

name: Lead(II) chloride solution
solubility: sparingly soluble cold, freely soluble hot
description: Lead(II) chloride that has gone into solution in hot water — and the fact that it does is what separates lead from silver. Solubility is not a fixed property of a substance; it is a property of a substance AT A TEMPERATURE, and lead chloride's rises steeply with heat where silver chloride's barely moves. Let this cool and needle-shaped crystals of the chloride come back out, which is a second confirmation in itself.
source: Vogel's Textbook of Qualitative Inorganic Analysis 5th ed. — Group I separation; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility against temperature)

name: Copper(II) sulfide
solubility: extremely insoluble, and insoluble even in dilute acid
description: A dense black solid, and so spectacularly insoluble that even dilute acid cannot pull it apart. That single fact is what makes the whole cation scheme work: copper's sulfide will precipitate from acid solution while zinc's will not, so passing hydrogen sulfide through an acidified solution separates one set of metals from another cleanly. It is also why copper is mined as a sulfide ore rather than found dissolved anywhere.
source: Vogel's Textbook of Qualitative Inorganic Analysis 5th ed. — Group II; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility product)

name: Zinc sulfide
solubility: insoluble in water but readily dissolved by dilute acid
description: A white sulfide, which is unusual — most metal sulfides are black or brown, and that alone half identifies it. The property that matters analytically is the opposite of copper sulfide's: dilute acid dissolves it easily, so it can only be precipitated once the solution has been made alkaline. Zinc sulfide also glows after being exposed to light, which is why it was the phosphor in glow-in-the-dark paint and in the screens of old televisions.
source: Vogel's Textbook of Qualitative Inorganic Analysis 5th ed. — Group IV; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility product)

name: Ammonium carbonate solution
description: The group reagent for the calcium, strontium and barium group, and it is chosen over sodium carbonate for a reason worth understanding. Sodium carbonate would precipitate magnesium as well and ruin the separation; ammonium carbonate used alongside ammonium chloride keeps the carbonate concentration low enough that only the least soluble carbonates come down, and magnesium stays in solution. The reagent is deliberately WEAKER than the obvious choice, and that is the whole point of it.
source: Vogel's Textbook of Qualitative Inorganic Analysis 5th ed. — Group V group reagent; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass)

name: Ethylmagnesium bromide (Grignard reagent)
description: A GRIGNARD REAGENT, and the thing that makes it useful is a reversal. In bromoethane the carbon attached to the bromine is slightly POSITIVE, because bromine pulls electrons away; put magnesium between them and that same carbon becomes slightly NEGATIVE. A carbon that was open to attack is now the attacker. That inversion is why Grignards build carbon–carbon bonds, and it is also why they destroy themselves on contact with water — a carbon carrying negative charge will grab a hydrogen ion from anything.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — organometallic chemistry; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass)

name: Magnesium hydroxybromide
description: The magnesium residue left after a Grignard reaction has been worked up with water or dilute acid. It is of no interest in itself — nobody makes a Grignard for this — but it has to appear in the equation, because the magnesium that did the work has to end up somewhere. Equations that stop at the organic product are telling you only half of what left the flask.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — Grignard work-up; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass)

name: Methanal solution (formalin)
description: The simplest aldehyde, and the only one whose carbonyl carbon carries TWO hydrogens rather than one. That makes it the odd member of the family in a way that matters: a Grignard added to it can only ever give a PRIMARY alcohol, where every other aldehyde gives a secondary one. Familiar as the preservative in biological specimens, and a carcinogen, which is why that use is now heavily restricted.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — carbonyl chemistry; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density)

name: Propan-1-ol
description: A PRIMARY alcohol — its carbon–OH group still carries two hydrogens. Count the carbons and compare with the bromoethane the Grignard was made from: two went in, three came out. A carbon–carbon bond has been built, which no reaction earlier in this app has managed. Being primary, it can still be oxidised twice over, to an aldehyde and then to an acid.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed.

name: Butan-2-ol
description: A SECONDARY alcohol — the carbon holding the OH has two other carbons on it and only one hydrogen left. That single hydrogen is the difference between this and the tertiary alcohol next door: it can be oxidised once, to a ketone, and then it stops. Made here from an ordinary aldehyde, and that is the general rule — aldehyde plus Grignard gives secondary, every time except with methanal.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed.

name: 2-methylbutan-2-ol
description: A TERTIARY alcohol: three carbons on the carbon holding the OH, and NO hydrogen left there at all. That absence is the whole of its character — with nothing to remove, ordinary oxidising agents cannot touch it, exactly as they could not touch a ketone for the same reason. Made from a ketone plus a Grignard, which completes the pattern: methanal gives primary, any other aldehyde gives secondary, a ketone gives tertiary.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed.

name: Propanoic acid
description: A carboxylic acid one carbon longer than the bromoethane it was built from, and that extra carbon came out of the air as carbon dioxide. Lengthening a carbon chain by exactly one is a genuinely useful thing to be able to do, and this is the standard way of doing it. Its salts are used to stop bread going mouldy.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, pKa 4.87); Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — carboxylation of Grignard reagents

name: Sodium borohydride solution
description: A MILD reducing agent, and mildness is the point of it. It delivers hydrogen to an aldehyde or a ketone and leaves esters, amides and carboxylic acids completely alone — so in a molecule containing several of those groups it will reduce exactly one of them. Being usable in water, unlike its aggressive cousin lithium aluminium hydride, makes it far easier to handle. Choosing a reagent for what it will NOT touch is one of the central skills of synthesis.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — chemoselectivity of hydride reducing agents; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass)

name: Lithium aluminium hydride in dry ether
description: The aggressive one. It reduces essentially every carbonyl group there is — aldehydes, ketones, esters, amides, and carboxylic acids that sodium borohydride cannot touch — which makes it powerful and unselective in the same breath. It cannot be used in water at all: it reacts violently, giving off hydrogen, so it is handled in dry ether and quenched with great care. Power and selectivity pull against each other, and this is the clearest illustration of it in organic chemistry.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — hydride reducing agents; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass)

name: Triiodomethane (iodoform)
description: Pale yellow crystals with a sharp antiseptic smell that anyone who has been in a hospital will half recognise — it was used as a wound dressing for decades before better antiseptics arrived. As a test result it is unusually informative: it appears only from a molecule carrying a CH₃CO— group directly on a carbon, or an alcohol that oxidises to one, so a positive result identifies a specific fragment rather than merely a family.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — the haloform reaction; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density)

name: Sodium iodide solution
description: Sodium iodide in water, here as the by-product of the iodoform reaction. Only one of the four iodine atoms used ends up in the yellow precipitate; the rest leave as iodide, which is worth noticing when the equation is balanced. Sodium iodide is also what is added to table salt to prevent goitre.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility)

name: Aluminium chloride (anhydrous)
description: The catalyst for both Friedel–Crafts reactions, and it works by being greedy for electrons. Aluminium here has only six electrons around it where it would prefer eight, so it grabs a chloride off whatever it meets and leaves behind a positively charged fragment hungry enough to attack a benzene ring. It must be bone dry: water destroys it instantly and violently, and damp aluminium chloride simply will not work.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — Lewis acids and Friedel–Crafts catalysis; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density)

name: Methylbenzene (toluene)
description: Benzene with a methyl group on it, and that small addition changes the ring's behaviour in two ways worth separating. The methyl group pushes electrons INTO the ring, so the ring becomes more reactive than benzene and any new group arriving is steered to the positions next to and opposite the methyl. Separately, the methyl group itself is now attackable in a way a lone benzene never is. It replaced benzene as a solvent because it is far less carcinogenic, though its vapour is still not something to breathe.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — substituent effects; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density)

name: Phenylethanone (acetophenone)
description: A ketone with a benzene ring on one side, made by Friedel–Crafts acylation. It is the reason acylation is preferred to alkylation in practice: the carbonyl group it installs pulls electrons OUT of the ring, deactivating it, so the product is less reactive than the starting material and the reaction stops cleanly after one substitution. Alkylation has the opposite problem. It smells strongly of sweet almonds and is used in perfumery.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — Friedel–Crafts acylation; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density)

name: 2- and 4-nitrotoluene
description: A MIXTURE of two products, not one compound, and the mixture is the result. The nitro group has gone to the position next to the methyl or the position opposite it, and essentially none has gone to the position in between. That pattern is what ortho–para directing means, and it happens because the methyl group pushes electrons into the ring and those electrons pile up at exactly those two kinds of position. Nitrating this further and once more gives TNT.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — directing effects in electrophilic aromatic substitution; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density of the 2-isomer)

name: 1,3-dinitrobenzene
description: Note where the second nitro group landed: the 3 position, in between — not next to and not opposite. That is META, and it is the exact opposite of what the methyl group produced. The nitro group already on the ring pulls electrons OUT, and it drains the next-to and opposite positions hardest, so the only place left with enough electron density to be attacked is the one in between. Directing effects are not arbitrary rules to memorise; they follow from where the electrons went.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — meta-directing deactivators; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density)

name: 2,4,6-tribromophenol
description: A white precipitate that appears the instant bromine water touches phenol — no catalyst, no heating, and THREE bromines at once rather than one. Benzene under the same conditions does nothing at all without a halogen carrier. That gap in reactivity is the measure of how strongly the OH group activates the ring, and the positions taken, 2, 4 and 6, are the ortho and para ones the OH steers everything to.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — activation by hydroxyl; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density)

name: 2,4,6-trinitrophenol (picric acid)
description: Bright yellow crystals, and two remarkable properties. It is a genuinely STRONG acid despite being a phenol, because three nitro groups pull so hard on the ring that the hydrogen comes off far more readily than an ordinary phenol's would — a substituent effect large enough to change what class of compound something behaves as. It is also a powerful explosive when dry, which is why laboratory stocks are kept deliberately wet and why a bottle found dried out is a job for the bomb squad rather than for a technician.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — substituent effects on acidity; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, pKa 0.38)

name: Benzoic acid
solubility: sparingly soluble cold, freely soluble hot
description: What is left when the methyl group of toluene is oxidised and the ring is not. However long the side chain was, oxidation cuts it back to a single COOH attached to the ring — so propylbenzene and methylbenzene both end up here. Its solubility rises steeply with temperature, which makes it the standard compound for teaching recrystallisation, and its sodium salt is a common food preservative.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — side-chain oxidation; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, solubility)

name: Phenylamine (aniline)
description: An amine attached to a benzene ring, and the compound that started the synthetic dye industry — every bright colour in Victorian clothing traces back to it. Its base strength is worth comparing with ammonia's: aniline is a much WEAKER base, because the nitrogen's lone pair is drawn into the ring and is no longer freely available to accept a hydrogen ion. The same donation into the ring is what makes the ring itself extremely reactive. It is absorbed straight through skin and is toxic, so gloves are not optional.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — aromatic amines; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density, pKb)

name: 2,4,6-tribromoaniline
description: A white precipitate, formed as instantly and as completely as phenol's did. Three bromines go on at once with no catalyst, because the nitrogen's lone pair floods the ring with electron density in the same way the oxygen's did. The positions are again 2, 4 and 6. Getting only ONE bromine onto aniline is genuinely difficult and needs the amine to be temporarily tamed first — being too reactive is a real problem in synthesis, not an advantage.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — activation by amino groups; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density)

name: Tin granules
description: A soft, low-melting metal, used here with hydrochloric acid as the classic reducing mixture for turning a nitro group into an amine. The tin goes from 0 to +4 and the four electrons it gives up are what do the reduction. Historically it is the metal that made bronze possible, and the metal that coats a tin can — where its job is simply to be less reactive than the steel underneath.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — reduction of nitroarenes

name: Tin(IV) chloride solution
description: What the tin becomes after it has done its job reducing a nitro group. It went from 0 to +4, and those four electrons are exactly what turned the nitro group into an amine — the reducing agent is oxidised, always, and following where its electrons went is how a redox equation is balanced. Its solution is acidic, because the small highly charged tin(IV) ion pulls hydrogen ions off the water around it, the same way aluminium does in alum.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — Sn/HCl reductions

name: Dioxovanadium(V) solution
description: Vanadium in its highest oxidation state, +5, and the starting point of the most famous colour sequence in inorganic chemistry. Vanadium is unusual in having four oxidation states that are all stable enough to sit in a beaker and all a different colour, so a single tube of it can be walked down the whole series by adding zinc and watching. The +5 state is the one vanadium(V) oxide uses to catalyse the Contact process.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — vanadium redox chemistry; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass)

name: Oxovanadium(IV) solution
description: Vanadium at +4, and the most stable of its four states — which is why this blue is the colour a vanadium solution drifts back to if it is left standing in air. Note that both this and the +5 state keep an oxygen firmly attached to the metal. The vanadium ion is small and highly charged enough that it holds on to an oxide ion rather than existing as a bare cation, and only at the lower oxidation states does that grip finally let go.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — vanadyl chemistry; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass)

name: Vanadium(III) solution
description: Vanadium at +3, and the first of its states to exist as a plain hydrated ion with no oxygen attached — the charge has dropped far enough that the metal no longer needs to hold an oxide. The green is easy to confuse with chromium(III)'s green, which is a useful reminder that colour narrows a possibility down rather than proving it.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — vanadium(III); CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass)

name: Vanadium(II) solution
description: Vanadium at +2, the end of the line and a powerful reducing agent in its own right — so powerful that it will pull oxygen straight out of the air and climb back up the series if the tube is left open. That instability is the point rather than a flaw: an ion is easy to make and hard to keep exactly when it wants its electrons somewhere else.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — vanadium(II) as a reducing agent; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass)

name: Chromium(II) solution
description: A bright blue that most students never see, because it does not last: chromium(II) is such a strong reducing agent that oxygen from the air oxidises it back to green chromium(III) within minutes of the tube being opened. Keeping it means keeping air out entirely. It is worth meeting once for what it demonstrates — that the oxidation states listed in a textbook are not all equally easy to hold on to.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — chromium(II) chemistry; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass)

name: Sodium tetrathionate solution
description: What two thiosulfate ions become when iodine takes an electron from each and joins them together through their sulfur atoms — four sulfurs in a chain where there were two separate pairs. It is the product that makes iodometric titration work, because it is colourless, stable, and forms in an exact two-to-one ratio with the iodine consumed.
source: Vogel's Textbook of Quantitative Chemical Analysis 6th ed. — iodometry; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass)

name: Sodium oxide
description: The first oxide of Period 3, and the most IONIC of them. Sodium hands its electrons over completely, so what is here is a lattice of separate sodium and oxide ions — and an oxide ion, once water reaches it, is a ferociously strong base. That is the whole reason this end of the period gives an alkaline solution: the bonding is ionic, and free oxide ions are what dissolve.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — Period 3 oxides; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density)

name: Phosphorus(V) oxide
description: The far end of Period 3, and the opposite of sodium oxide in every way that matters. Phosphorus and oxygen have similar enough pulls on electrons that they SHARE them, so this is not a lattice of ions but separate covalent molecules — which is why it melts low and dissolves rather than merely reacting at a surface. Its appetite for water is so extreme that it is used as a drying agent, and it will strip water out of compounds that were not offering any.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — Period 3 oxides; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density)

name: Silicon tetrachloride
description: A colourless liquid that fumes the moment the stopper comes off, because the water vapour in the room is enough to start it hydrolysing. The reason silicon does this and carbon does not is worth knowing: silicon is a bigger atom with empty d orbitals available, so a water molecule can attach itself before any bond has to break. Tetrachloromethane, its carbon equivalent, has nowhere for the water to get a hold and is famously unreactive with it.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — Period 3 chlorides; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density)

name: Sodium silicate solution (water glass)
description: What silica becomes when hot concentrated alkali finally breaks its network apart. That it takes such harsh conditions is the point: silica is an acidic oxide, but a very weak one, and the giant covalent structure has to be dismantled bond by bond before anything can dissolve. Known as water glass, and used to preserve eggs, to fireproof timber and to make silica gel.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — silicates; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density)

name: Aluminium chloride solution
description: A solution of a salt that has no business being acidic, and is. Neither aluminium nor chloride looks like an acid, but the Al³⁺ ion is small and carries three charges, so it pulls hard enough on the water molecules around it to force hydrogen ions off them. That is the same effect that makes alum work as a coagulant, and the same reason magnesium chloride is faintly acidic while sodium chloride is not: it tracks the charge and size of the metal ion, straight across the period.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — hydrolysis of metal aqua ions; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass)

name: Sodium nitrite solution
description: Never used as it comes. Mixed with cold acid it makes nitrous acid, which is too unstable to keep in a bottle and is therefore generated in the flask at the moment it is needed — a common arrangement for a reagent that will not survive being stored. Sodium nitrite is also the curing salt that keeps ham pink and stops botulism, which is why a compound this toxic is nonetheless in the food supply.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — diazotisation; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass)

name: Nitrous acid
description: A weak acid that cannot be bottled: left to itself it falls apart into nitrogen oxides and water, and it does so faster the warmer it gets. That is why it is always made in the flask from sodium nitrite and acid, in the cold, immediately before use. A reagent generated where it is needed rather than poured from a bottle is a normal answer to instability, not a special case.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — nitrous acid; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, pKa 3.4)

name: Benzenediazonium chloride solution
description: Two nitrogen atoms held on a benzene ring by a bond that barely wants to be there. The whole of its usefulness comes from that reluctance: nitrogen gas is such a stable thing to become that this group will leave in favour of almost anything, so it is the doorway from an amine to a very large number of other compounds. The same reluctance is why it cannot be kept — above about 5 °C it falls apart on its own, and the dry solid is explosive. It is made cold, in solution, and used within minutes.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — diazonium salts; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass)

name: 4-(phenyldiazenyl)phenol (an azo dye)
description: An AZO DYE, and the reason its colour is so intense is structural. Two benzene rings joined through a nitrogen–nitrogen double bond make one continuous system of shared electrons running the whole length of the molecule, and a long system like that absorbs visible light rather than ultraviolet. Make the system longer or hang different groups off the ends and the colour shifts — which is why azo compounds account for most synthetic dyes in use, and why the first of them turned an industry from boiling plants into building molecules.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — azo coupling and dyes; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass)

name: 4-(phenyldiazenyl)aniline (an azo dye)
description: The same azo backbone as the orange dye with an —NH₂ on the far ring instead of an —OH, and the colour has moved from orange to red. Nothing else about the molecule has changed. That is the whole principle of dye design in one comparison: the coupled system decides that there IS a colour, and the groups hanging off the ends decide which one, so a chemist adjusts a shade by changing a substituent rather than by starting again.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — azo dyes and colour; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass)

name: Iodobenzene
description: Iodine on a benzene ring — a compound that cannot be made by the direct route at all. Chlorine and bromine can be put onto a ring with a halogen carrier; iodine is too unreactive for that to work. Going the long way round through a diazonium salt is how it is actually done, which is a good illustration of why chemists build multi-step routes rather than always looking for the shortest one.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — aryl halides from diazonium salts; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density)

name: Cotton cloth
description: Cellulose, which is the same glucose units the starch batch met, joined a different way round — and that one difference in the link is why cotton is a fibre you can weave and starch is food you can digest. Its molar mass is null for the honest reason: different cellulose chains are different lengths. What matters for dyeing is that the chains lie alongside each other in a tangle with gaps a flat dye molecule can lodge in.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — cellulose and fibres

name: Dyed cotton cloth
formula: cellulose with dye held in it
description: Cloth with dye lodged in it, and the wording matters: the dye is HELD, not bonded. Nothing has reacted. Flat dye molecules have slipped between the cellulose chains and are kept there by the same weak attractions that hold any two surfaces together, which is exactly why a direct dye like this fades with washing. Reactive dyes, invented much later, form a real covalent bond to the fibre and do not.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — direct and reactive dyes

name: Poly(ethene)
solubility: insoluble in water and in almost everything else
description: The most-made plastic on earth: carrier bags, bottles, buckets. It has no single molar mass — different chains stop at different lengths, so the question has no one answer, which is true of every polymer here. Chemically it is nothing but a very long alkane, and that is exactly the problem: alkanes are famously unreactive, so nothing in the environment has an easy way to attack it. The property that makes it useful and the property that makes it persist are the same property.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — addition polymerisation; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (density)

name: Chloroethene (vinyl chloride)
description: Ethene with one hydrogen swapped for a chlorine, and still carrying the C=C that lets it polymerise. It is a proven human carcinogen — it causes a rare liver cancer, discovered among workers in PVC plants in the 1970s, and that discovery is why the monomer is now handled in closed systems. The finished PVC is not itself a carcinogen; the danger is in the monomer and in any of it left unreacted.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — addition polymers; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, gas density)

name: Poly(chloroethene), PVC
description: Drainpipes, window frames, floor tiles and electrical insulation. On its own it is rigid and brittle; adding a plasticiser — small molecules that sit between the chains and let them slide past each other — turns the same polymer into something as floppy as a shower curtain. That is worth noticing: the properties of a plastic are not fixed by its formula alone. Burning it is the real hazard, because the chlorine leaves as hydrogen chloride.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — addition polymers; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (density)

name: Phenylethene (styrene)
description: Ethene with a benzene ring on it, and both halves matter. The C=C is what polymerises; the ring is what ends up sticking out along the finished chain, getting in the way of the chains packing neatly together. That awkwardness is exactly why polystyrene is rigid and glassy rather than waxy like poly(ethene) — a bulky side group is a real, physical obstruction.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — addition polymers; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density)

name: Poly(phenylethene), polystyrene
description: Rigid and glassy where poly(ethene) is waxy, because the benzene rings hanging off every other carbon stop the chains packing closely together. Blown full of gas it becomes the expanded foam used for cups and packaging, which is more than 95 % air — the same molecule, in a different physical form, doing a completely different job.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — addition polymers; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (density)

name: Tetrafluoroethene
description: Ethene with every hydrogen replaced by fluorine. The C=C is still there, so it polymerises like any other alkene — but the carbon–fluorine bond it carries into the polymer is the strongest single bond carbon forms with anything, and that one fact decides everything about the material it becomes.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — fluoropolymers; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, gas density)

name: Poly(tetrafluoroethene), PTFE
description: The non-stick coating on a frying pan, and the most chemically inert plastic there is — acids, alkalis and solvents all leave it alone. The reason is the carbon–fluorine bond: it is the strongest single bond carbon forms, and the fluorines form a tight sheath along the outside of the chain that shields the carbon backbone from anything trying to reach it. Non-stick is that inertness made useful, and it was found by accident, when a cylinder of the gas polymerised itself in storage.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — fluoropolymers; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (density)

name: Benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid
description: A benzene ring with a COOH group at each end — and having TWO of them is the whole point. A molecule with one reactive group can only ever join to one partner and stop; a molecule with two can join at both ends and keep going, which is what turns a reaction into a polymerisation. Chemists call that being bifunctional, and it is the requirement every condensation polymer is built on.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — condensation polymers; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density)

name: Poly(ethylene terephthalate), PET
description: Drinks bottles and polyester fabric, and the links holding it together are ordinary ester groups — the same C(=O)O link met when ethanol and ethanoic acid were warmed together, just repeated thousands of times. Because they are ester links, hot alkali can hydrolyse them apart again, which is why PET can genuinely be broken back down to its monomers and rebuilt. That is a chemical difference from poly(ethene), not a difference in how hard anyone is trying.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — polyesters; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (density)

name: 1,6-diaminohexane
description: A six-carbon chain with an —NH₂ group at each end: bifunctional, like the dicarboxylic acid, and for the same reason. Its solution is alkaline because an amine is a base. The six carbons are not arbitrary — the exact chain length decides how neatly the finished nylon chains pack against each other, and that packing is what gives the fibre its strength.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — polyamides; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density)

name: Hexanedioyl dichloride
description: An acid chloride at BOTH ends of a six-carbon chain. The dicarboxylic acid would eventually make nylon too, but only on prolonged heating; using the acid chloride instead makes the reaction fast enough to happen at room temperature the moment the two solutions touch. Trading a harsher reagent for gentler conditions is a routine piece of synthetic thinking, and here it is what makes the classroom demonstration possible.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — interfacial polymerisation; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density)

name: Nylon-6,6
description: A POLYAMIDE: the links along its chain are amide links, the same C(=O)N bond that joins amino acids into a protein. Nylon is, structurally, a synthetic protein with a very boring repeating unit — and it is strong for the same reason silk is, because the N—H on one chain hydrogen bonds to the C=O on the next and pulls the chains tightly together. The name 6,6 counts the carbons in each monomer: six in the amine, six in the acid.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — polyamides; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (density)

name: Aminoethanoic acid (glycine)
solubility: very soluble (about 25 g per 100 mL at 25 °C)
description: The simplest amino acid, and bifunctional in an unusual way: it carries an acid group AND a base group on the same small molecule, so it can join to another copy of itself at either end. That is why one compound alone can polymerise where a polyester needs two different monomers. In solution most of it exists as a zwitterion, with the hydrogen already moved from the acid end to the amine end — an ion that is positive and negative at once and neutral overall.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — amino acids and peptides; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, solubility)

name: Polypeptide
description: Amino acids joined into a chain by amide links — which is to say, a protein, or at least the backbone of one. Put this beside the nylon made two entries earlier and the links are the same kind of bond, formed the same way, losing a molecule of water each time. The difference is that nylon repeats one dull unit forever while a real protein draws on twenty different amino acids in a specific order, and that order is what makes one protein an enzyme and another a hair.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — peptide bond formation

name: Sodium terephthalate solution
description: What the acid half of a polyester becomes once hot alkali has hydrolysed the chain apart — the salt rather than the free acid, because the alkali immediately takes the hydrogen. Acidify it and the dicarboxylic acid comes back out, ready to be polymerised again. That round trip is what chemical recycling of PET actually is, as opposed to melting bottles down and hoping.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — hydrolysis of polyesters; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass)

name: Ziegler–Natta catalyst
description: A MIXTURE — a titanium halide together with an aluminium alkyl — so it has no molar mass of its own, like Fehling's and biuret reagent. It is what makes addition polymerisation practical: without it poly(ethene) needs something like two thousand atmospheres, and with it the same polymer forms at ordinary pressure. It does more than speed things up, too. It holds each monomer in a fixed orientation as it joins, so the side groups end up arranged regularly along the chain rather than at random, and a regular chain packs tightly and gives a stronger, denser plastic. Ziegler and Natta shared the 1963 Nobel Prize for it.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — Ziegler–Natta polymerisation; Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — organometallic catalysis

name: 2-methylbuta-1,3-diene (isoprene)
description: A DIENE — it carries TWO carbon-to-carbon double bonds, not one, and that is the whole reason rubber can be what it is. Polymerising uses up only one of them; the other survives into the finished chain. Everything rubber can do that poly(ethene) cannot, and everything that goes wrong with it, traces back to that leftover double bond. It is also the unit nature builds rubber from, and the same five-carbon block it uses for terpenes and steroids.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — diene polymerisation; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density)

name: Natural rubber latex
solubility: a stable dispersion, not a true solution
description: The milky sap that runs from a cut in a rubber tree. The rubber is already fully polymerised inside it — the tree does that, not the factory — and what arrives at the plantation shed is tiny particles of rubber held apart in water by a coat of protein. It has no molar mass because it is a dispersion of a polymer, not a compound. Left alone it stays milky for days; the whole of harvesting is persuading those particles to stop repelling each other and clump.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — natural rubber; Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Macromolecules

name: Natural rubber (polyisoprene)
solubility: insoluble in water, but dissolves in benzene and similar solvents
description: Raw rubber, and on its own a disappointing material: sticky when warm, brittle when cold, and it dissolves in petrol. Its long chains are coiled and can slide past one another, which is what lets it stretch — and also what lets it flow and stay stretched instead of springing back. Every one of those faults is fixed by tying the chains to each other, which is what the sulfur is for. Note it still carries a double bond in every repeat unit; that is where the sulfur will attach.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — natural rubber and vulcanisation; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (density)

name: Vulcanised rubber
solubility: insoluble in everything — it swells instead of dissolving
description: Rubber with short sulfur bridges tying its chains to one another, and the change in the material is out of all proportion to how few of them there are — roughly one cross-link per few hundred units is enough. The chains can still uncoil when pulled, so it stretches; they can no longer slide past each other and stay put, so it springs back. It is a THERMOSET: with every chain tied into one giant network, there is nothing left that can dissolve or melt, so it swells and then chars rather than flowing.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — vulcanisation and cross-linking

name: Rubber solution
description: Raw rubber dissolved, which it can be because its chains are separate objects — solvent gets between them and carries them off one at a time. This is what rubber cement and bicycle puncture glue are, and it is also exactly what vulcanised rubber can no longer do. A polymer that dissolves is telling you its chains are not tied to each other.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — thermoplastic versus thermoset behaviour

name: Brominated rubber
formula: polyisoprene with Br2 added across its double bonds
description: What rubber becomes when bromine adds across the double bonds left along its chain. The product itself is of no use to anybody — the point is that it forms at all, because it proves those double bonds are really still there after polymerisation. A material can be tested for unsaturation exactly like a small alkene can.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — unsaturation in polydienes

name: Ozone
description: Oxygen with three atoms instead of two, and far more aggressive for it — the third atom is held weakly and comes off readily to attack whatever is nearby. High in the atmosphere that reactivity is what absorbs ultraviolet and shields the surface; at ground level, where it forms in photochemical smog, the same reactivity damages lungs and crops and quietly destroys rubber. Bent, not linear, and it has a faint sharp smell noticeable after a thunderstorm.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — ozone; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, gas density)

name: Perished rubber
description: A rubber band left in a drawer for a year: grey, hard, and it snaps instead of stretching. Ozone in ordinary air has attacked the double bonds along the chains and cut them, and a shorter chain cannot coil and uncoil the way a long one could. The same double bond that made vulcanisation possible is the weak point that lets this happen — a structural feature is rarely only an advantage, and here the strength and the flaw are the same bond.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — ozonolysis and rubber degradation

name: Bakelite (phenol–methanal resin)
description: The first fully synthetic plastic, from 1907, and still used for saucepan handles and electrical fittings because it does not soften when hot. Its chemistry has nothing in common with rubber's — it is a condensation polymer of phenol and methanal, and the phenol rings are joined in three directions rather than two, so the whole solid is one continuous network with no separate chains in it at all. Reaching the same thermoset behaviour by a completely different route is the point of meeting it here.
source: Clayden, Greeves & Warren, Organic Chemistry 2nd ed. — phenolic resins and thermosets

name: Dimethyldichlorosilane
description: Silicon carrying two methyl groups and TWO chlorines, and the count of those chlorines is the only thing that matters about it. Each one becomes an —OH when water reaches it, so two chlorines means two —OH groups, which means a molecule that can join at both ends and build a chain. It is the same bifunctional requirement the polyester and the nylon needed, arriving here on a silicon atom instead of a carbon one.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — silicones; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density)

name: Dimethylsilanediol
description: TWO —OH groups on one silicon, which is exactly what a monomer needs to build a chain: one end joins forward, the other joins back. It will not sit still for long — silanols condense with each other readily, which is why this is made and used rather than stored.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — silanols; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass)

name: Silicone (polydimethylsiloxane)
description: Bathroom sealant, oven-glove lining, medical tubing. Its backbone is not carbon at all — it alternates silicon and oxygen, and that single substitution is why it does things an organic polymer cannot. The Si—O bond is considerably stronger than C—C, so it survives temperatures that char polythene; and the methyl groups point outward all along the chain, presenting a greasy surface to the world, which is why water beads off it.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — polysiloxanes; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (density)

name: Trimethylchlorosilane
description: Three methyl groups and only ONE chlorine — so hydrolysis leaves it with a single —OH, and a molecule with one reactive end can join to one partner and then it is finished. It cannot build a chain. That makes it useless as a monomer and genuinely useful as a chain STOPPER: added to a silicone mixture it caps a growing chain and halts it, which is how the chain length, and therefore the thickness of a silicone oil, is controlled.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — chain termination in silicones; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density)

name: Trimethylsilanol
description: ONE —OH group, and that is the whole story. Put it beside dimethylsilanediol with its two and the difference in what they can build is total: two —OH groups make a chain, one makes a dead end. It is the clearest demonstration in the app that the number of reactive groups, not their nature, decides whether polymerisation is even possible.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — silanols; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density)

name: Methyltrichlorosilane
description: One methyl group and THREE chlorines, so hydrolysis gives three —OH groups on one silicon. Three reactive ends cannot make a chain — a chain needs exactly two — so what it builds instead branches in three directions and closes into a network. The parallel with Bakelite is exact, and reached from an entirely different starting point: three reactive positions rather than two is what turns a polymer into a thermoset.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — silicone resins; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density)

name: Methylsilanetriol
description: THREE —OH groups on one silicon. Count them against the diol's two and the mono-ol's one, because those three numbers are the whole of this batch's first half: one gives a dead end, two give a chain, three give a network. Nothing about the chemistry of the —OH group changes between them.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — silanols and network formation; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass)

name: Silicone resin
description: A silicone that has branched in three directions instead of running in a line, so the whole solid is one connected network — a thermoset, like Bakelite and like vulcanised rubber, and insoluble and unmeltable for the same reason all three are. It is used where heat resistance and hardness are both wanted at once: electrical insulation, and the paint on things that get hot.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — silicone resins
