name: Soda-lime glass
solubility: insoluble in water and in almost every acid
description: Windows and bottles, and an inorganic polymer in the strict sense: a silica network with its bonds broken up here and there by sodium and calcium ions, which is what lets it soften gradually instead of melting at one sharp temperature. Its formula is written approximately on purpose, because glass is not a compound with a fixed composition. It is also not a solid in the usual sense — its atoms never settled into a regular lattice as it cooled, so structurally it is closer to a liquid that stopped moving.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — silicate glasses; Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Common chemical industries, glass

name: Dry clay (kaolinite)
solubility: insoluble in water, but swells and softens in it
description: Kaolinite, the clay mineral pottery is made from, and structurally it is sheets — layers of aluminium and silicon oxide stacked like paper, held to each other only weakly. Water slides between those sheets and lets them slip past one another, which is exactly why wet clay can be shaped and why dry clay is powder rather than rock. Note the OH groups in the formula: those are chemically bonded water, and driving them out is what firing does.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — layer silicates; Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Common chemical industries, ceramics

name: Plastic clay
formula: Al2Si2O5(OH)4 with water between the sheets
description: Clay you can throw on a wheel. Nothing has reacted — water has simply worked its way between the mineral sheets and is acting as a lubricant, letting them slide over each other and stay wherever they are pushed. That is why the change is completely reversible: let it dry and the water leaves, and it is dry clay again. Firing is what makes the change permanent, and firing is chemistry rather than drying.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — clay plasticity

name: Metakaolin
description: What clay becomes once the chemically bonded OH groups have been driven off as steam — the first firing stage, and the point of no return. The neat layered structure has collapsed into a disordered one, and because the OH groups are gone there is nothing left for water to reattach to. This is already irreversible; the second firing stage that follows only makes it hard as well.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — dehydroxylation of clay minerals

name: Mullite (fired ceramic)
solubility: insoluble in water and in most acids
description: The mineral that makes fired pottery hard, and it does not exist in the clay you started with — high temperature builds it. Needle-shaped mullite crystals grow through the fired body and interlock, in much the same way the crystals in setting cement do, and glassy silica fills the gaps between them. That interlocking is the strength of a fired pot, and it is why the pot is a different material from the clay rather than a dried version of it.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — mullite formation in ceramics

name: Calcium silicate slag
description: What forms when a basic oxide meets an acidic one at furnace temperature — and in a blast furnace that is deliberate, because slag floats on the molten iron and carries the impurities off. The same reaction is a disaster when the acidic oxide is the furnace LINING rather than the charge, because then it is the wall being eaten. Whether this reaction is useful or ruinous depends entirely on which silica it consumed.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — acid-base behaviour of oxides in slags

name: Magnesium silicate (forsterite)
description: A basic oxide and an acidic one reacting again, with the roles the other way round: here it is the magnesia lining being eaten by silica in the charge. The lesson is that neither kind of lining is simply better. A refractory is only refractory relative to what you put next to it, and choosing one is a question about the process rather than about the material on its own.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — refractory attack by slags

name: Gypsum
description: Calcium sulfate with two water molecules built into its crystal, mined as rock and used for plasterboard. The water is not damp — it sits at fixed positions in the lattice, which is what makes this a hydrate rather than a wet solid, and why removing it takes a furnace rather than a towel.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Common chemical industries

name: Plaster of Paris
solubility: sparingly soluble, setting rather than dissolving
description: Gypsum with three quarters of its water driven off — a HALF molecule per formula unit, which is unusual enough to be worth noticing and is not a rounding. Add water back and it sets hard in minutes, which is why it is used for casts and mouldings. The half-water state is what makes it work: enough structure is left to rebuild the crystal quickly, and enough is missing that it is desperate to.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Punjab Curriculum and Textbook Board, Chemistry XII — Common chemical industries

name: Zinc oxide
description: What roasting turns zinc blende into, and the form the metal is actually won from — carbon can pull oxygen off a metal, so an oxide is the useful intermediate whatever the ore started as. It has a memorable trick of its own: white when cold and yellow when hot, reversibly, because heating knocks a few oxide ions out of the lattice and the gaps left behind absorb light. It is also the white in calamine lotion and in sunscreen.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — zinc extraction; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density)

name: Iron(III) oxide (haematite)
description: Haematite, the main ore of iron, and the same compound as the rust on a gate — which is a fair summary of why steel needs painting. Extracting iron is the business of putting back the electrons that rusting took away, and the whole blast furnace exists to do that on a scale of thousands of tonnes a day.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — iron extraction; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density)

name: Carbon monoxide
description: The gas that does the actual reducing in a blast furnace, and the reason a blocked flue kills people. It has no colour and no smell at all, so there is nothing to warn you, and it binds to haemoglobin far more tightly than oxygen does — so the blood keeps circulating while carrying nothing useful. The victim feels sleepy rather than breathless, which is why so many die without waking.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — carbon monoxide as a reducing agent; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, gas density)

name: Copper(I) sulfide (chalcocite)
description: A copper ore, and the one that does something no other ore in this batch manages: blown with air it reduces ITSELF to the metal, with no carbon and no separate reducing step. The sulfide in it is oxidised to sulfur dioxide and, in the same breath, hands over the electrons that turn the copper ions into copper. It is part of why copper was among the first metals people ever smelted.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — copper extraction; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density)

name: Mercury(II) oxide
description: An oxide so reluctant to exist that gentle heating alone tears it apart — no carbon, no reducing agent, nothing but a flame. That is what sitting at the very bottom of the reactivity series means in practice. It matters historically twice over: this is the compound Priestley heated in 1774 to discover oxygen, and Lavoisier's work on the same reaction is what overturned phlogiston. Mercury and its compounds are cumulative poisons that damage the nervous system permanently.
source: Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — thermal stability of metal oxides; CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density)

name: Mercury
description: The only metal that is liquid at room temperature, and dense enough that lead floats on it. It is also seriously poisonous in a way that is easy to underestimate: it evaporates slowly at room temperature, the vapour has no smell, and what it does to the nervous system builds up and does not reverse. A spilt thermometer is a genuine clean-up problem, not a curiosity to push around with a finger.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); PubChem, National Library of Medicine — Mercury

name: Gold
solubility: insoluble in water and in every single acid
description: The bottom of the reactivity series, and the practical meaning of that is simply this: gold is found as gold. It does not corrode, it does not tarnish, and no single acid will touch it — which is why a gold coin comes out of a shipwreck looking new while an iron nail beside it has gone entirely. It also needed no extraction chemistry at all to be used, which is why gold and copper were worked thousands of years before iron.
source: CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed. (molar mass, density); Housecroft & Sharpe, Inorganic Chemistry 4th ed. — the coinage metals
